### ledger-boot-load — the ledger's first load runs in the fold worker; no reader loads it in its own tick (on usage-relearn-stepped round 2; 主开发 22:29Z)
- **The reader (the owner's journal, named on a scratch hub).** 20 s after boot the pool engine's first anchor sweep (usage-pool-engine `setTimeout(sweepUsageAnchors, 20000)`) asks the whole-ledger gate, whose `prime()` → the estimator's primeIfCold → `_primePairs` → `_evCountUpTo(Infinity)` → `_sortedEvents` → `_loadEvents` loaded the WHOLE ledger in that one call: every line parsed and hashed (`idHash`, the whole-line staleness mark), 12.2 s on the owner's 717 MB; 13.2–13.8 s on the lane's 664 MB / 2.2 M-row scratch ledger.
- **The road (src/usage-history.js).** The hub's ledger (server.js: `firstLoadInWorker: true`) takes its FIRST load in the fold worker — the road a reload already took (B-748f: `_requestRebuild` → usage-cold-worker.js `_packWhole` → `_stageBuilt` a chunk a turn → `_swapCache`). Until it lands the cache is an EMPTY placeholder marked `booting`: every sync reader answers from it and `ledgerLoading()` says `{booting, bytesLeft}` — asking it IS an ask (it starts the load), so a reader that checks before it reads is never told «whole» over an empty list. The async readers wait for it (`_waitBigWarm` ⇒ `_bootWait`: the try under way; inside a failed try's backoff, code LOADING at once); the gate's `whenWarm` waits for it (`bootLoadSettled`, never rejects). The boot warm joins it. No line is parsed or hashed on the loop, at boot or after a reload; the migration's own instance (ledger-slot-backfill) keeps the named synchronous load, inside the boot's synchronous step.
- **Rows that arrive during the load.** No row ever enters the placeholder: a turn's commit or a device's batch appends to its shard (the ingest index dedups a re-send by rid), the worker's marks say how far it read, and the swap's `checkedAt = 0` makes the next reader's pass read the rest — rows the worker read are in its build, rows after its read in that pass, a re-written line deduped by rid: each once. A reader between the append and the swap sees the empty «loading» cache.
- **What a person sees while it loads.** The usage window: «Loading…» (its request waits for the try under way — round 2: never longer) and then the whole ledger's figures; a failed try ⇒ «Could not load usage: … the usage ledger is still loading … retry». The pool ring: the last quota reading's percent (a reading, not the ledger), no estimate ring or «est» chip while the ledger loads and its first learn primes. A message's popup: its billing row comes when rid-info answers (it waits for the load); a failed try ⇒ rid-info `{found:false, loading:true}` and the row says «the usage ledger is still loading» (was «not in the ledger yet»: a real answer's words). No message cost row reads the ledger (the chip is the CLI's own total_cost_usd; `_cost` × pricing only feeds the live estimate). Diagnostics shows no ledger totals; a failed first load is its `usage-first-load-failed` event.
- **A worker that fails** (exits mid-pack, runs out of memory, throws): said ONCE by its cause — «the ledger's first load in the fold worker failed (the fold worker exited (9)) — the usage figures say «loading»; it is tried again after 5 s, then doubling to ≤ 2 min — never parsed on the main loop» — and one Diagnostics event; asks inside the backoff start nothing; the next ask after it tries once; a waiter (the gate, the warm) asks again by itself when the backoff ends; the try that lands says «(try N; the failure said above)». Never a synchronous load as the fallback.
- **The pool holds** from the first ask until the gate opens — the ledger whole and its first learn primed (commit B's hold): the worker's wall time (14.7–15.4 s at 664 MB) + the hand-over (0.6–0.75 s) + the prime (2.3 s) — 18.1 s measured from the first sweep (+20.2 s) to the prime's end (+38.3 s); the base road about 16 s (its 13.7–13.8 s load in one turn, then the same prime). A wall inside that window: the automatic decision is held (`holds()`), and onWhole decides every auto pool again — once.
- **The hand-over's cost (664 MB, 2.2 M rows, three boots).** The loop's longest turn while the worker reads: 14–23 ms; during the hand-over: 10–16 ms (465 chunks; with the CPU profiler attached once 92 ms — the turn that receives the worker's message, its non-transferred parts cloned); after the swap ≤ 46 ms (a GC, the prime's steps). Peak RSS 1.55–1.62 GB (the base road: 1.46–1.47 GB); the worker's own heap peaked at 785–790 MB used and is gone at the swap. Round 2, the memory said truthfully (the panel at 198 MB: 614 / 619 MB against 466 / 480): the process's peak is about a third above the release's while the worker loads — about +0.5 GB for some 15 s at a 700 MB ledger — and the main heap's own peak goes DOWN (the worker is another isolate): the main heap's 4.2 GB is not the limit, the box's memory is.
- **Round 2 (主开发 08:44Z — the panel: 11 of 12 scenes hold; one moderate).** A FAILED FIRST LOAD MADE THE REAL ROUTES WAIT FOR EVER: the scan awaited whenWarm() → bootLoadSettled(), which resolved only when a try LANDED; while tries failed the scan stayed pending, so GET /api/usage-stats and the rid / mid lookups (scan(); await scanSettled() first) never reached the LOADING answer, every later scan() answered skipped (the hub's turns not added — not lost: the cursors did not move) and the pool's 30 s tick added an awaiting closure each time; round 1's ④ stubbed the scan, which hid it. THE LAW — nothing waits on a load that is failing: the scan waits for the try under way only and otherwise walks on, its commit deduped by the shards' tails; bootLoadSettled() resolves when the try under way ends, or inside a backoff when the next try ends (the gate looks again — one wait at a time); the boot warm's trace span alone waits for the landing (bootLoadLanded); the shard judge drops its kick after a failed try (judged again at the next ingest). PIN ⑦ through the REAL scan and the route's own sequence (a transcript walked): a worker that throws on every try — the route and the rid lookup answer LOADING with the cause and the next try, three times in 2 ms each, each new local turn reaches the ledger, no scan left pending; the worker heals — the next try lands (≈ 0.3 s) and the route's figures equal the release's road (9 881 requests); RED, the wait unbounded again: the route pending. The panel's own drivers on this tree: failscan — the route LOADING at 87 ms (round 1: pending); tree-later — route, rid and mid LOADING at 500 ms; tree-heal with one new ask after the heal — 2 000 requests in 76 ms.
- **The follow-up (主开发 09:36Z — round 2 ACCEPTED as 9822bdada, a pick; the failing load's edges in a commit on top, in the train's order on 0dd72da0d).** (1) A TRY THAT HANGS (the worker neither answers nor dies) held every reader and the scan until the fold deadline — ten minutes a try: a reader now waits for the try under way at most BOOT_READER_WAIT_MS = 10 s (`_withinTry`: the scan, the async readers, the gate's wait), then LOADING while the try goes on («… has run N s and goes on; ask again at HH:MM:SSZ», `nextTryAt`, `running`). (2) A PERSON'S RETRY is attended: the Usage window's Retry sends retry=1 and the route calls `retryBootLoad()` — the first load is tried now, never after the unattended backoff (5 s doubling ≤ 2 min). (3) LOADING IS A STATE in the window: the route answers `{code: 'LOADING', nextTryAt, running}` (503, its words as `error` — other callers unchanged); the window shows «The usage ledger is still loading — next try at HH:MM:SS» (`ledgerLoadingOf`, usage-ledger-note.js; zh, ja), no error toast, and asks again by itself at that time (cleared at close). (4) THE POOL'S WORDS: `ledgerLoading()` carries the failure (`failed`, `fails`, `nextTryAt`); the whole-ledger gate says it ONCE with its cause and the heal once; the kb states what the pool does meanwhile (the automatic decision skipped, the anchor sweep waiting; manual switches and the wall machine's verdicts go on). (5) usage: «N folds ahead» counts the folds tied in the turn's comparator — the turn's own stable sort. Pins: test-ledger-boot-load ⑧ through the REAL route handler (account-usage-routes on a fake app) and the real scan — a hung worker: LOADING after the bound, the turn in the ledger (RED: the reader waits for the try itself — pending); the press inside a 5 s backoff lands in ≈ 0.1 s, through the route too (RED: the backoff kept — no try); the window's state and words (pure) and its wiring; the gate's failure and heal lines once (RED: no failure line); test-usage-relearn-cap §24: qq behind 6 folds (RED: the ties uncounted — 5).
- **The follow-up's amend (主开发 11:11Z — 11 of 15 scenes held; one moderate).** A CLOSED USAGE WINDOW KEPT ASKING: onClose cleared the re-ask timer, but a LOADING answer that landed after the close armed it again (and every later one), for the page's life; reopened beside it, two loops; the harvest's reply could start a load after the close. THE LAW (the listener lifecycle): a window's timers and the continuations of its requests end with it — `alive()` (closed first in onClose) checked by load before it asks and after its await, by the re-ask, the pivot ask and the harvest's reply. Pinned on the REAL page: test-usage-window-pivots §7 — the real route over a hung first load, a LOADING answer held in flight across the close ⇒ 0 asks after it, reopened ⇒ one loop; CONTROL alive() always true ⇒ asks after the close, two loops. SMALL: (1) ONE budget a request — the scan's wait and the reader's share the try's deadline (start + 10 s; in series they held 20 s; RED: each its own 400 ms ⇒ pending); (2) a person's press replaces the re-arm timer (RED: the old one left — an unattended try at its old time); (3) the kb: darkSources reads the gate (its list never memoized while loading — the wall's switches and the pinned placements decide with no dark-host pessimism until the landing); (4) test-fixture-isolation's census follows a NAMED CONSTANT into a spawn( call (`const SRV = path.join(wt, 'server.js')`, `spawn(node, [SRV], …)`), with a CONTROL; a constant that only names the file is not a spawn. The suite split under the fast tier's 10 s: ⑦ + ⑧ — the failing first load's road — in scripts/test-ledger-boot-fail.mjs.

- **Pins.** test-ledger-boot-load (new, fast): ① the first second — every sync reader «loading»/empty, 0 lines parsed or hashed on the loop (RED: the flag off — the first ask parses every line; and 5c77612ef = 2.369.393, run on a copy of that tree); ② the cache after the load byte for byte the synchronous load's (hrh + cold rh, rids/mids), the route's totals, a cost sum; ③ rows before the worker's read, after it, a device's batch + its re-send, a re-written line: once (RED: a swap that keeps a re-check time); ④ exit / out of memory / a throw: said once, no line on the loop through three tries, backoff 5 s → 10 s, LOADING to async readers, a waiter's retry lands (RED: a sync fallback); ⑤ a wall at +50 ms held, onWhole once after the swap on the whole ledger (RED: a ledger that does not say it is loading); ⑥ the wiring (the hub's flag, the migration's sync road in the listen callback's synchronous step, its three calls and no other, rid-info + the popup words). test-ledger-rebuild's census: `_bootLoad` declared (an empty placeholder).

### sidebar-echo-order — an echo never undoes what the person did after it was asked; the later act wins, as on master (the owner's incident inc-mwbn2xp8-ks0b, 2026-11-11: «我的批量操作一直在回滚»)
- **The incident (measured from the bundle's action + WebSocket rings).** 122 inline Archive clicks in 55 s on a hub whose loop lagged (median 1 902 ms over 3 min, level 2). The FIRST `user-state-updated` echo reached the page 44.3 s after the first click (107 clicks made by then); 73 echoes followed over 76 s, 67 after the last click. Each echo REPLACED the page's whole sets with what the server held when THAT broadcast was made (src/lib/sidebar.js → `_applyServerState`), its own echo included; the next click PATCHed the changed top-level key WHOLE (B-b87b's belt diffed top-level keys only), so the rolled-back list erased on the server what the echo had rolled back on the screen.
- **The order: the server's write counter `stateRev`, within the server's life `stateEpoch`.** stateRev is persisted in user-state.json, +1 on every write (ops, a whole-key PATCH, an older page's POST, the config import, the server's own archive + rename); stateEpoch is one id per process start, `ep<start>-<random>` (a page orders lives by their start — a GET answered by the life before a restart and arriving after it is the past; a restore, a LOWER counter, starts a later life and is taken). Both ride in the GET body, every broadcast's `state` and every answer; they are the server's, never data (normalizeUserState keeps them out of the person's keys, a client-sent one is ignored, the config export leaves them out). A state that names no life (an older server) is taken as it comes — the overlay keeps the page's own acts.
- **The page: base + pending (PURE src/user-state-ops.js `createSync`).** The page shows the newest server state of the server's life (an echo at or below it changes nothing, no re-render) PLUS its own acts the server has not confirmed; an act leaves the overlay only with every act before it (the confirmed PREFIX). A push carries what the person changed — per item; per MEMBER inside a group (sessionGroups, groupFolders); per FIELD inside a conversation's config (sessionConfigs — B-fe9c inside one conversation too).
- **Every act is on the wire at the act, in a request that carries everything the page has not seen confirmed.** One act = one batch (an act past 5 000 ops, 1 MiB or 512 KiB of values = its parts — 20 000 ops before round 12), its id the page's (made per page LOAD, in memory) + a counter, handed to the network at once — also before the first GET — in `{batches: [{batch, age, ops}, …]}` carrying EVERY batch of the page no answer has confirmed, oldest first: master's redundancy, in ops (a later act carries an earlier one whose request failed or was late). Each batch carries its AGE: the device's WALL clock between the act and this send (never negative) — a difference on ONE device, so no two devices' clocks are ever compared. An answer from another server life confirms nothing: the page asks for the state and sends again. Nothing about an act is stored or shared between pages.
- **THE LAW (round 7, 主开发): an act is dropped only if someone else changed the item after the act was made; the later act wins, as on master.** The route keeps ONE FACT PER SLOT (an item; a member of a group; a field of a config; a group itself) that a write changed in the last 7 days: `{t: the ACT's time — now − age, never ahead of now (round 8: a fact stamped when it LANDED let the first to land after an outage stand); now for a whole-key writer, the page + its act counter, prev: up to 4 other pages' acts on it}`. An op of page P, act counter c, is judged at the hub's now: no fact ⇒ applied; the slot last changed by P ⇒ applied when c is above that act's counter (P's own next act), else held (a duplicate — on disk); P in the fact's prev with c not above ⇒ superseded (a copy of an act another writer beat, its age short by its transit — not on disk, so never «held»); another writer ⇒ applied when now − age ≥ t (a tie: the later arrival wins, as on master), else dropped — the page shows the server's value, nothing said. A fact ahead of now is read as now. An act older than 7 days is not applied — its page takes it back once it shows the server's state, and says so only where what it shows changes — unless the server holds it (its fact names it, or the state holds exactly what it writes: held, judged by its own slots — round 10, MUST 2) or a later act beat it (superseded, nothing said): «not kept» is never said of what is on disk. THE CLOCKS (round 8): the hub's clock is HIGH-WATER — a wall clock stepped back reads as the mark plus the MONOTONIC time since (its fractions carried — round 9), until the wall catches up; the mark is persisted (`stateClock`), TAKEN AT BOOT (round 9, MUST 2: the state read and the clock taken once before the routes serve — a step back after a restart and before the first write no longer loses the idle time), and a life starts at or after it; the page's age is the larger of the wall and the monotonic difference (the wall for a sleeper — a monotonic timer stops while a laptop sleeps; the monotonic one where the wall was set back). A fact older than 7 days is dropped AT A WRITE, never on the read path. Batches are judged in the body's order, the facts moving batch by batch; the ops of one act against the facts as they stood before it. A group delete is judged per slot (each member goes unless a later act decided it; the group itself goes unless another writer changed it later — and goes whole when it was not there before the act); a member added to a group another writer deleted after the add was made is dropped (the later delete wins).
- **An omission by a writer that carries no facts is not an act (round 9, MUST 4).** A whole-key write by a page that predates the ops door (a tab still on an older bundle — its PATCH, or its POST before its first fetch) states what it SETS; what it merely does not contain is its ignorance — the slot's fact is kept, marked omitted, and the act it removed, re-sent by a page that knows facts (its own counter), applies over it. The owner's first minutes after an update: a .392 tab's stale whole key no longer turns a new page's waiting acts into «superseded» (N1..N10 and Y all on disk). The price, named (round 10: wider than round 9 said): a factless writer's removal of an item is undone by ANY waiting act on that item made after the item's last fact — another page's too, even one made before the removal; master's next whole-key push carried the item back the same way.
- **A batch id names ONE act (round 9).** Each owner fact keeps its act's digest (FNV-1a over its ops); the same id with OTHER ops — another op beside a shared slot, or another value on it — is refused by name (`reused-id`); the same ops are its own re-send. Round 10: the prev entries keep their act's digest too, so an id whose act's only slot moved to another page's prev is still its ops.
- **The rows first, then the word (round 10, MUST 1).** Whenever an answer changes what the page shows — a refusal, the 7-day rule, an act another writer beat, a later state taking an act back — `createSync` tells the page so (`onView(view, 'answer')`) and the sidebar repaints its rows in that same task; a word is said only after the rows show it (round 9 re-painted at the next render: the sentence came over rows that still showed the act).
- **«This page now shows the server's» is true (round 10, MUST 2).** (a) A week-old act the state holds EXACTLY — every slot it writes already holds what it writes — is confirmed silently (held), judged by its own slots: a set key's members are read once per REQUEST, never per batch (S1c: 2 000 such acts against 20 000 vs 40 000 conversations ×1.01). (b) An answer that names week-old acts for a state NEWER than the page's base takes nothing back yet: the page asks for that state (one GET), shows it, and only then takes the acts back — saying the sentence where what it shows changed, the row showing the other device's value; never the page's own older base under the server's name. An act another writer beat, answered for a newer state, fetches it too (with the socket down, the GET is the only road).
- **A person's config import is an ACT at its time (round 10, MUST 3).** `POST /api/config/import` replaces each user-state key whole and sets a KEY-WIDE fact (`'<tag>\t*'`, t = now): an op made before it, re-sent after it, is dropped (the import stands, nothing said); an act made after it is judged as always. A .392 tab's whole key (`POST` / `PATCH /api/user-state`) stays an omission (round 9).
- **A request is bounded by its op count (round 10, MUST 4).** At most MAX_OPS_PER_REQUEST ops in all (20 000 in round 10 — one full select-all batch; 5 000 since round 12, below); the page sends the oldest batches that fit and the rest at the answer (the road the byte bound already takes); the route refuses more by name (400 `too-many-ops`, the file unchanged). A batch refused on its own counts nothing toward it. Found on the way and made LINEAR (round 9 had them too): the judge re-applied a whole group per member op (20 000 adds to one group: 23 s — a group is now an ordered set kept as the request goes), a held week-old member add scanned its group (a Set per group, per request), applyOps copied a conversation's config per field op (20 000 fields: 92 s — once per call now). Pinned: the group shapes in WORK (×2.01); the field shape TIMED at the bound against a select-all measured beside it (≤ 5×; round 9's per-op copy reads ×600).
- **Smaller (round 10).** A value nested deeper than the depth bound (32 levels then, 4 since round 12) is refused at the PAGE, alone (said once), before it rides with other acts the route would then refuse whole. ONE bound for the fact's writer and reader: a counter of at most 15 digits (always a safe integer), a fact of at most 480 characters (the longest the writer makes is 456: five 64-character page ids with their 15-digit counters and 7-character digests, a time to the year 9999) — the worst legal fact is written and read back in the suite.
- **The deferral asks until the state comes (rounds 11–13).** (a) A page with no state yet has a base older than any answer: a week-old act it is told of waits, the page asks, and takes it back at its first state — never «this page now shows the server's» over its local display copy. (b) While an act waits for a state (a week-old one; one another writer beat, answered for a later state) the page ASKS — at once, then 2 s, 5 s, 15 s … — ONE ask in flight at a time (round 11 let three overlap: in a browser without AbortSignal.timeout forty hung GETs filled the six connections the acts need), each given up through the engine's own timer and an AbortController after 15 s, 30 s, 60 s, then 2 min — the give-up lengthens with the pace (a hub answering the GET in 20 s satisfied no 15 s ask); past 40 asks it keeps asking once every 5 min for as long as an act waits (round 11 stopped at 40: the network back with no reconnect and no broadcast left the person's value on the row for good); a state the page takes starts the count again and ends a 5-minute wait at once, a paced one keeping its time. Round 13: one ask in flight also while a second deferral comes (pinned — round 12 left that guard unpinned); a hub slower than the 2-min give-up never satisfies an ask (named). Round 10 asked once.
- **One value is bounded (round 11, MUST 2).** One VALUE is at most MAX_VALUE_CHARS = 16 384 characters — the owner's largest real value is 139 (a group's members), a config field 79 (poolPin), a name 42 — refused by name (`too-large-value`) at the page (alone, said once) and at the route; the walk that measures it is ONE walk (depth and size together) that stops at the first bound it passes (round 10 walked a value twice, whole: one config field of 1.5 M keys held the hub 9 s, a 24 M-element array 16 s — master 2.9 s / 0.9 s for the same content); round 12 counts it exactly as JSON.stringify(value, null, 2) writes it, 8 spaces a line. A name (item / member) is at most ITEM_MAX 4 096 characters and the fact reader's slot bound is derived from it (round 10's reader skipped slot keys past 4 200: a group and a member of 3 000 characters wrote a fact the boot dropped). A write compares the keys it changed entry by entry (round 10 stringified both whole keys); the digest is fed as the ops' JSON without building it (byte-identical, pinned over random op lists). Round 11's body bound (12 MiB, checked by the handlers against the content-length) and its table are replaced by round 12's, below.
- **No name spells another slot (rounds 11–12).** The import's key-wide slot is `'<tag>\t'` (no name), a group's own slot `'<tag>\t<item>\t'` (an empty member), a group's tombstone `'<tag>\t<item>\t-'`; every name inside a slot is spelled by its LENGTH — `<length>:<name>`, or `<length>#<64-bit digest>:` past 128 characters — so no name spells another slot and none is scanned (round 10's `'<tag>\t*'` made one rename of an item named `*` act as an import over the whole key, `+` spelled a group's own slot, a tab inside a name another item's member; round 11 escaped `\` and the tab with two regex replaces at every slot).
- **Smaller (round 11).** A refusal is said only where what the page shows changes (as the 7-day rule): an act a later act of the page on the same item masks is undone with nothing to see (round 12: two refused acts on one item in one answer say it once). The judge's ordered-set group is pinned member by member (a remove, a re-add, a delete with a member kept). NAMED, with the verifier's number (round 11 said 6.3 s — the engine alone, at the wrong count): each act's request carries every unconfirmed batch (round 5, up to 5 000 since round 12) and the view is base + every pending act — 5 000 one-op acts made with the network down cost the real page 61 s in all on round 11, 91 s and 3.7 GB on round 12, ~36 s and 453 MiB since round 13 (13.5 ms a click at 4 000–5 000 waiting; the engine alone 12 s; master's page 6.4 s).
- **THE OPS DOOR IS BOUNDED, AND ITS BOUND CANNOT BE STEPPED AROUND; MASTER'S ROADS TAKE WHAT MASTER TAKES (rounds 12–13 — 主开发's laws).**
  - THE OPS DOOR (`PATCH /api/user-state/batches`, this release's pages — the one road that judges per op) takes at most 5 000 ops a request and a batch, 2 MiB of body and 512 KiB of values.
  - Every op there is held to its own bounds, each refused by name: one value ≤ 16 384 characters as JSON.stringify(value, null, 2) writes it, 8 spaces a line (`too-large-value`); 4 levels deep (`too-deep` — the product's deepest value is 2, a config's tools {allow, deny}); a name ≤ 4 096 characters (`not-a-name`); a field name ≤ 200; a group ≤ 20 000 members (`too-large-group`).
  - The page's splitter reads the same numbers, and what the page will not send it refuses itself, before any road carries it.
  - Its bytes are counted AS READ by its own parser — a chunked body, and a gzip body by what it inflates to — and refused by name (413 `too-large`) before the handler.
  - server.js skips its 50 MB parser for exactly the paths that parser's layer matches: the router's own compiled match (any letter case, a trailing slash). Round 12's own regex in server.js missed '/api/user-state/batches/' and '/API/USER-STATE/BATCHES', and a 41 MB ops request landed in 487 ms.
  - MASTER'S ROADS — the whole-key PATCH / POST (a tab still on an older page), the import, and the server's own writers (the ws rename) — take what master takes: no bound master does not have, and master's parser.
  - Past 20 000 changed items, a whole-key write is recorded as ONE RECORD for each key it changed, never refused. Round 14: the record holds the 64-bit digests of the slots that write changed, so it takes back an earlier act on one of THOSE items only — never one on an item it did not touch (below).
  - Two shapes stay refused at the whole-key PATCH — the two named exceptions to «master's roads take what master takes»: an array body (400 `Expected object`), and a body naming `batches` / `ops` / `born` / `seq` / `stateBatches` (400, by name). The release stored both as junk keys, and no page of the release sends either (every caller read). An import drops a stored top-level `batches` / `born` / `seq` / `stateBatches` (the four wire keys) from an export's user state.
  - What round 12 cost on those roads: it held them to every bound. A person's own export then refused to import — every section of it, not only user state — when the stored state held a value, a name, a depth or a group past them, and master's doors and this release's own ws rename could put one there. An old tab was blocked by data it never sent.
- **Law A — never worse than master on the same content.**
  - The measurement: one run, both trees, the handler alone, median of 3, a socket client that takes the frame's bytes. The comparator is master's same door; for the ops door, it is master's whole-key PATCH leaving the same state. The limit is 1.25 × master, or 100 ms where master is under 80. All in ms, tree / master.
  - THE OPS DOOR — the laws, every row under the 100 ms floor: 5 000 archives 44.8 / 2.1; 5 000 member adds 54.6 / 2.1; 5 000 fields 57.3 / 1.8; 5 000 adds into a group of 15 000 66.1 / 7.8 (the thinnest); a group of 20 000 deleted 27.9 / 0.2; 512 KiB of renames 5.3 / 1.9; 512 KiB of values at their bound 8.0 / 4.5; 512 KiB at depth 4 4.4 / 1.4; 2 MiB of names 21.2 / 3.5, of tabs 21.0 / 6.8, of backslashes 19.3 / 5.7.
  - MASTER'S ROADS (measured, no bound), the whole-key door:
    - 12 MiB of values at their bound 105.5 / 204.9 (×0.51); at depth 4 206.2 / 611.6 (×0.34); tab names 44.0 / 47.0 (×0.94); renames 39.5 / 41.5 (×0.95).
    - An old tab's select-all of 20 000 51.5 / 8.7 (under 100), of 25 000 25.5 / 10.8 (under 100: the key's record of 25 000 digests); a group of 25 000 made whole 26.6 / 9.1.
    - An old tab's ONE change on 66 670 archived ids 29.2 / 24.8 (×1.18), on 270 000 ids 144.3 / 149.2 (×0.97). Round 12 read ×2.0–2.45 there: the whole key was diffed through two Sets. Since round 13 the common head and tail are skipped position by position and a few changed items looked up.
    - BEYOND 10× THE OWNER'S STORE (measured, the panel's driver, 5 runs): 20 000 items changed on a 12 MiB key (≈ 270 000 ids) — round 13 295 / 134 ms (×2.2, the panel's: two Sets of the whole key and every fact encoded twice); now 20 000 new 182 / 113 (PATCH) and 197 / 140 (POST), ×1.4–1.6 (a fact a slot); past 20 000 (the key's record) 20 001 new ×1.11 / ×1.19, 25 000 new ×1.37 / ×1.21; 20 000 or 25 000 removed ×1.00–1.18 (no act). 40 MiB of new ids (≈ 840 000, 100× the owner's store): the handler alone 870–940 / 535–585 ms, ×1.5–1.6 (round 13 650–670, ×1.2); over HTTP with a socket client 1 040–1 170 / 620–730, ×1.6–1.8 (round 13 ×1.23–1.30, the panel's) — the record's 840 000 digests, and 12.8 MiB more in user-state.json for up to 7 days.
  - THE IMPORT: 10× the owner's store 42.0 / 36.1 (×1.16); 12 MiB of values 102.3 / 206.9 (×0.49); 270 000 ids 123.8 / 158.3 (×0.78).
  - With lib9's socket client (it parses every frame inside the clock — the panels' harness; round 13's run): values ×0.71; tabs ×1.29 and renames ×1.95, both under 100; the import's values ×0.72 and ids ×0.92; the one change on 270 000 ids ×0.97–1.33 over four runs (the client's 12 MiB parse is most of both).
  - The cure that made a write of values cheaper than master's: ONE STRINGIFY A WRITE. Master stringifies a write's whole state twice, pretty for its file and compact for its broadcast. user-state.json is written compact, and the broadcast's state is the same text — byte for byte what the old frame carried.
  - The cuts at the ops door: a name in a slot is spelled by its LENGTH (no escape, no scan; past 128 characters a 64-bit digest), a slot is built once per op, a group taken whole is one fact (its tombstone), and the value walk is one pass. Round 14: a wide list change is diffed by its changed middles, and a changed fact is encoded once.
  - logs: the lane's bench law-a-r14.log (one run, every row above but the BEYOND ones; round 13's law-a-r13-parse.log for the parsing client); the BEYOND rows logs/kept14/store/logs/a12-12ids-r14c.log, scenes-big*-r14c-*.log and logs/bench14/whole40.mjs.
- **Law B — what the product's own pages and tools send stays under 250 ms (the lane's box, a socket client attached).**
  - A select-all of 2 000 (the owner's size): one request.
  - A select-all of 20 000: four requests of 5 000, about 45–60 ms each, in act order, no part sent twice — also with its own answers and echoes coming back. Round 12 re-sent the part in flight at every echo and every answer: 18 requests, 5.3 MiB more. The page drives the four parts once each and the person's own acts beside them.
  - The largest group the product can build (20 000 members in one act): four requests, the last adding 5 000 to 15 000 — 76 ms.
  - An old tab's select-all of 25 000 through its whole key: the key's record, 26 ms.
  - An import at 10× the owner's store (66 670 archived, 7 530 names, 320 configs; 3.6 MiB) in ONE request: 42 ms.
  - Pinned in scripts/test-user-state-bounds.mjs against the largest legal import measured in the same run (≈ 90–150 ms on the lane's box): each under 2× it, the ops door's law A rows under 1.5× it.
- **The page never contradicts itself (round 13).**
  - What the page will not send — a value, a depth or a name past the ops door's bounds, a group grown past 20 000 by what it shows — it refuses BEFORE any road carries it, said as THIS page's: «This page did not keep a change (…)». A refusal that came back from the server is still «The server refused a change (…), so it was undone here».
  - A harness that writes a rename back (codex) used to record the op (refused at the page) AND send the ws rename-session, whose server writer (master's road) stored the very name the page had just called undone.
  - Each reason has its words (a group larger than 20 000 conversations; more changed values than one request carries). Two refusals with two reasons in one answer are two sentences; two with one reason stay one.
  - A group past 20 000 is refused at the page whole — round 12's splitter let the parts around the refused one land: 19 999 of 20 001.
  - The page's own cost:
    - 5 000 one-op acts made with the network down: 35.6 s of page CPU in all and a heap of 387 MiB — master's page 6.55 s and 68 MiB (the panel's run; the lane read 35.9 s and 453 MiB). A click costs about 14 ms at 5 000 waiting and 22 ms at 7 000 (master about 2.6 ms). Each act's cost is linear in the backlog, as master's is (every act's request carries every unconfirmed batch, up to 5 000; master's carries the whole key) — and past 5 000 it still grows, with the state the page copies for its view (round 14: named, not cut).
    - Round 12 measured 91 s and 3.7 GB: an arrow over the backlog inside issue() made it context-allocated, so every request's timer and answer kept a snapshot of the whole backlog.
    - The page now applies base + pending once per change (round 12 copied the whole state four or five times an act) and diffs an act without copying either side.
- **An act is taken back only for a reason about ITS OWN item (round 14 — 主开发's law; round 13's sentence withdrawn).**
  - Round 13 wrote, past 20 000 changed items, ONE fact for the whole key dated at arrival — and the judge then dropped EVERY earlier act on that key, whatever its item, silently: a person's archive of X, made on an updated page and still on its way, was taken back by an old tab's select-all of 20 001 that never touched X (at 20 000 it was kept). The release keeps X.
  - Now the key's record (`'<tag>	*'`) holds the 64-bit digest (two FNV-1a lanes, about 57 effective bits — a false positive per act at 100 000 digests ~7e-13, the panel's measure) of every slot the write changed — and the tombstone of a group it deleted — and reads, for each of THOSE slots only, as the fact moveFacts would have written there (`{t: the write's time, page: none}`); an act on any other item applies. One record a key, in RUNS — one a write, each at its own time, a digest in its newest run only; a run older than 7 days goes (no act that old is applied), at the key's next record and at the hourly sweep.
  - THE OMISSION RULE IS JUDGED FIRST, AT EVERY SIZE: a stale whole key's removals are no acts (round 13 counted them before the rule, so a stale key omitting 20 001 items became a key-wide act). A stale key that only omits takes back nothing.
  - Its cost: a run is one typed table (two 32-bit lanes a digest), its text 16 hex characters a slot. Making it cheap cut two older costs too: a wide list change is diffed by its changed MIDDLES (the head and tail are the same in both lists; round 13 built two Sets of the whole key — an old tab's 20 000 new ids on a 12 MiB key cost ×2.2 master's), and a changed fact is encoded once, not twice.
 writeUserState: each slot whose value the write changes — by a page's op (its page and counter) or by a whole-key writer (an old page, desktop-app-prefs, the config import, the server's own archive / rename: no page) — gets `{t: now, writer, prev}`; an applied op decides its slot even where the value was already so; a request that changed no value writes its facts alone (no new rev, no broadcast, no hook). There is no memory per page, so no page is ever forgotten: an act before the first GET, a tab idle for weeks, a counter that went back all simply land.
- **C1 — ops only.** A page of this release speaks ops to `PATCH /api/user-state/batches` and nothing else; a refused or absent door (404 — a relay's own while the hub restarts, or an older VibeSpace —, 5xx, a network error) is a failure like any other: the act kept and sent again within the bounds. Round 14: a 404 from the ops door is not a verdict for 3 minutes (the minute of an update: a reloaded tab talks to the old server until the restart, then every act lands); a 404 streak past that is SAID once — «These changes are not saved yet — the server does not take them (it may be restarting or older than this page); they are kept here while this page stays open» (zh / ja) — never «reload» (acts live in this page's memory: a reload loses them), and taken back when they land («The changes kept on this page are saved now»). Against a downgraded server the acts stayed on screen, never landed, and vanished at a reload with no word. There is no older-server mode and no whole-key fallback. `PATCH /api/user-state` takes whole keys (an old page, desktop-app-prefs, the panels' folds); ops there are refused by name. The load drops a top-level `batches` / `born` / `seq` / `stateBatches` an earlier build stored.
- **C2 — nothing on the read path writes over what was read.** A state READ whole is the state served; the normalizer's own rewrite (legacy refs, a stored junk key) is tried on its own and, should the disk refuse it (a full disk, a read-only data dir), said once in the log — never the default served because a WRITE failed. The first write that lands drops the junk.
- **«Once» is on disk before it is said.** The state, stateRev and the facts are ONE atomic write; the cache and the facts change only once it is on disk — a write that fails moves neither (503 by name; the page keeps the act as not saved).
- **The page speaks ONLY when it takes something back on the screen (round 9, MUST 1 — a cut).** An act is shown at once and re-sent while the page stays open; there is no word about waiting and none about arriving — every false word of eight rounds came from «not saved yet» / «saved» (round 8's «15 s from the oldest act» met the 32-request cap and said «not saved yet» of acts on disk). What is said: a REFUSAL, from the CODE the route sends (`refused: [{batch, error, code}]`, a 400's `code`), worded by the page in en / zh / ja — «The server refused a change (a value it does not take), so it was undone here»; and the 7-DAY RULE, one neutral sentence true whether the act was never applied or applied once and beaten since — «A change made more than 7 days ago was not kept — this page now shows the server's» — said only where what the page shows changed because of it. A 401 waits for the next answered state and says nothing (signing in is the app's, as on master).
- **JUDGING a request costs its ops (round 9, MUST 3; writing it joins every kept fact — below).** Judging is linear in the request's ops: the reused-id check reads an index the draft keeps as it goes (round 8 spread the draft's changes per batch: one request of 20 000 one-op batches 1 212 ms, 40 000: 5 501 ms — now 151 / 306 ms, round 7's 101 / 219); the groups a request touches are kept as it goes; an old batch is judged by its own slots, never by the store (round 8 re-applied the request's ops per old batch: the incident's 122 clicks 8 days old against 20 000 conversations 591 ms, 500 such batches 2 271 ms — now 0–1 ms). (Round 9's bound let a request of ≈ 359 500 one-op batches through: 4.4 s on the hub's thread — round 10 bounds a request at 20 000 ops, round 11 at 12 MiB, round 12 at 5 000 ops and 2 MiB at the ops door.) Pinned in WORK (scripts/work-meter.mjs): ×2.01 for ×2 batches; ×1.00 for ×2 the store.
- **A write ENCODES only what it changed (round 8) — and JOINS every kept fact (round 13, the sentence corrected).**
  - The judge runs on an OVERLAY of the facts (nothing copied); once the write is on disk, only the slots it changed are committed and encoded.
  - Every write still writes the facts' part whole — a join of every slot's kept text — so a write costs O(facts), and only their 7-day age bounds them.
  - Measured (a one-op rename at the ops door, the person's state empty, the facts left by legal archive / un-archive pairs): 2 541 facts — a real week at the owner's size (2 000 conversations, a select-all, 200 renames, 40 stars, 300 config fields) is 2 540 — 1.2 ms and a 0.2 MiB file; 30 001 11 ms (2.4 MiB); 100 001 31 ms (8.2 MiB); 360 001 103 ms (29.5 MiB). Master: 0.1 ms, no facts.
  - Bench, one-op PATCH at 20 000 facts: round 7 47 ms → round 8 10 ms.
- **A refusal is settled on both sides.** A batch with a bad op, no op, or past 5 000 ops (20 000 before round 12) is refused ON ITS OWN, by name (`refused: [{batch, error}]`, 200 — the others apply); so is a batch id taken before arriving with OTHER ops (round 8: a batch id names one act). The page undoes it, shows that, and then says it (a whole sentence, also with no reason). A malformed body is refused whole, by name (400; a value nested deeper than 32 levels — round 8, before it overflowed the write's stack as a 503; 413 past 48 MiB).
- **A request that fits goes KEEPALIVE (round 15 — the .397 hosted mirror).**
  - The train's hosted runner ran test-user-state-echo-chrome red on both tries: five quick acts and the tab closed at once — the hub received four of five, then two. All five requests were on their way («in flight: 5»), and the browser CANCELS a closing tab's plain request still uploading. Master's page loses the same acts: it sends a plain fetch per act too, and nothing at pagehide. The box was fast enough that every upload beat the close.
  - Now a request whose body fits goes with `keepalive: true` — the browser completes it after the tab is gone. The budget is the page's keepalive bodies in flight, at most 48 KiB, under the browser's 64 KiB a page (shared with the telemetry beacons). Past it — a select-all's parts, about 500 archives or more — the plain fetch, as on master, and that road is named. A keepalive the browser refuses (its quota, or the network) falls back to the plain fetch in the same send: never a dropped act (a duplicate is held by its batch id). The law (主开发): an act a person made is handed to the browser in a way that outlives the page, whenever it fits.
  - Nothing is stored for a next page: an act still lives and dies with its page; a closed tab's keepalive requests simply reach the hub.
  - The harness now models the browser: a closed tab's plain request still on its way is cancelled, a keepalive one lands (rounds 4–14 let every one land — which is why only real Chrome on a slower machine showed it).
  - Measured, the real page in headless Chrome with its CPU throttled through CDP, five acts and the tab closed at once (acts landed of 5, three runs each): on the lane's box no CDP condition separates the three trees — the page's CPU throttled ×1 / ×4 / ×8 / ×16 / ×32, its network latency 0 / 200 / 500 / 1000 ms, each request HELD inside Chrome (CDP Fetch, the request stage) 0 / 150 / 400 / 1000 ms: 15 of 15 acts landed at every step on the release, on 8c1612cf0 and on the fix, but once — the release, 12 of 15 at 0 ms latency (one run lost its third archive, the star and the rename). The box's Chrome 154 lets a closed tab's dispatched requests finish — even plain ones held inside it; the hosted runner's Chrome did not (four, then two of five). The hosted mirror is the judge.
- **Nothing waits, and nothing is said about waiting.** Each request has a 15 s bound (this hub holds its loop up to ~10 s several times a day). A request past it, answered 5xx / 404, or never reached, is LATE: the page's next act carries it, or ONE paced re-send at a time (2 s, 5 s, then 15 s; round 14: a request sent meanwhile — an echo's — cancels the pace, so a backlog never has two windows in flight) — at most 40 in a row (≈ 10 min; the next act, a reconnect or a state starts them again), with at most 32 requests listened to at once. A reconnect sends one request at once. A 401 / 403 waits for the next answered state; the page says nothing (round 9). The owner's scene: 121 requests for 120 clicks with the first answer 44 s late — 123 with the socket dropped and re-made in the middle; 0 whole-key requests, 0 words.
- **What a request may carry (主开发's rulings, rounds 12–13).**
  - The ops door: ≤ 5 000 ops, ≤ 2 MiB, ≤ 512 KiB of values; one value ≤ 16 384 characters, 4 levels deep; a name ≤ 4 096 characters; a field name ≤ 200; a group ≤ 20 000 members.
  - Master's roads (the whole-key doors, the import): what master takes.
  - Past one request's worth, the oldest go and the rest at their answer, one window at a time; a page closed before then loses the rest. Master's whole-key body carried up to 50 MiB ≈ 1.1 M ids.
  - applyOps is LINEAR (the work meter: ×2.00 for ×2 input).
- **The facts' bytes, at the owner's shape.** A fact on disk is `'<t base 36>:<page>:<counter>[:<page>:<counter>]…'` under its slot. 2 000 conversations and a busy week — a select-all, 200 renames, 40 stars, 300 config fields: 2 540 facts, 214 KB in user-state.json (84 B a fact — each name in a slot now carries its length) beside the state's 124 KB, the whole file 338 KB, written compact since round 12; only slots changed in the last 7 days are kept. The facts a hub can hold are master's (none) or this release's: round 10's and round 11's spellings never shipped, so there is nothing to carry — both directions with master are pinned (the rollback cells write master's file over this one and come back; the restart legs read master's file).
- **The census of the other user-state writers.** Covered by the law: the sidebar's eight keys (archive, star, rename, mode, config, legacy groups, folder-archive, the key migration — which runs on the first SERVER state only) and the Manage-mode batch. Staying last-write-wins per key, named (single-control page prefs, not per-conversation state; each write gets a rev and moves the facts of what it changed): channels-panel `channelsNoticesSeen` / `channelsPanelFolds`, jobs-panel `jobsPanelFolds`, window-share's reach map, owner-facts' page facts, desktop-app-launcher's recents, desktop-app-prefs (already read-before-write); the server's own setCustomName / archive helpers read-modify-write on the server. The storage census: every localStorage / sessionStorage write in src/lib is one master makes (114, by file, call and key).
- **How it got here (fifteen rounds).**
  - Rounds 1–4: round 1 coalesced acts behind one request in flight; round 2 stored the unsent ones in localStorage for a later page to replay; round 3 handed the unsent ones over at pagehide in one keepalive request; round 4 sent every act alone and made the server commute them by per-slot deciders.
  - Rounds 5–7: round 5 gave back master's redundancy (a request carries everything the page has not seen confirmed); round 6 made a per-PAGE memory of «once» true on disk — a memory that had to forget, and forgetting made four holes; round 7 withdrew it: a fact per slot, each act judged by its age — the later act wins.
  - Rounds 8–9: round 8 made «Saved» true, dated a fact by its act, kept the clocks honest and made a write encode only what it changed; round 9 CUT the waiting / arriving words (the page speaks only when it takes something back), took the clock mark at boot, made a request cost its ops, stopped treating a factless writer's omission as an act, and tied an id to its ops.
  - Rounds 10–11: round 10 painted the rows before every word, said the 7-day sentence only over the server's state, made an import an act, bounded a request by its op count, and gave the fact's writer and reader one bound; round 11 made the deferral ask until the state comes (also with no base), bounded one value, and let no name spell another slot.
  - Round 12 held every door to every bound at the bytes it reads, wrote each state with one stringify, and let a select-all of 20 000 go in four requests.
  - Round 13 withdraws half of that: master's roads take what master takes. The ops door's bound is matched by the router's own match. The page refuses what it will not send before any road and says it as its own, and stops re-sending the part in flight and keeping the backlog per request.
  - Round 15 (the .397 hosted mirror): a request that fits goes keepalive — a closing tab's plain request still uploading is cancelled by the browser, on master too.
  - Round 14 withdraws round 13's key-wide fact: a whole-key record names the items it changed, the omission rule comes first at every size, and a wide list change is diffed by its middles. The fork-title road refuses before the window's title, a server without the ops door is said after 3 minutes (never «reload») and taken back when the acts land, and a paced re-send never goes beside a window in flight.

an old tab saves over it; an old tab's select-all of 25 000 lands as one record; a whole key of 13.6 MB taken); law A's and law B's rows (a select-all of 20 000 in four requests, in order, no part sent twice — also with its answers and echoes coming back) against the largest legal import measured in the same run; round 14, each red on 06d30d218: the verifier's scene at 20 000 / 20 001 / 25 000 and across a restart (X kept, Y taken back by the write's own change, Z kept), a stale key that only omits takes back nothing at every size, each write keeps its time (two runs), a run past a week goes, a group deleted past the bound keeps its tombstone, and the record's cheap paths equal the plain ones (slot digests fed by parts; a list diffed by its middles, with duplicates). Five bounds removed and ten moved (the lane's mutants) each turn a leg red by name — never a hang, an out-of-memory or a RangeError. scripts/test-user-state-echo-chrome.mjs (heavy): five acts and the tab closed at once — the hub receives every one, each once.
- **Named limits (a person's sentences).**
  - A change your browser had not yet sent (a burst past the browser's six connections to one site) is lost if the page closes first, as on master.
  - A change whose request is larger than 48 KiB — a select-all of about 500 conversations or more, or a change sent while such a request still waits for its answer (it rides along) — is lost if the tab closes before it reaches the server, as on master. A smaller one reaches the server after the tab is gone.
  - A change made while the server is down is lost if the page closes before it comes back, as on master.
   - When a page holds more than one request's worth of changes the server has not confirmed (5 000 changes, 2 MiB of them, or 512 KiB of their values), the rest goes only after an answer; closing the page before then loses it. Master's body carried up to 50 MiB.
   - A tab still on the release before this one writes through master's road and takes what master takes. Past 20 000 changed items its write is one record for the key naming the items it changed: a change another page made before it to one of THOSE items, still on its way, does not land over it; a change to any other item lands.
   - A tab still on the release before this one, left open across the update, sends its whole list as it last saw it: conversations this page had archived, starred or renamed since (and the server confirmed) can drop out of the list on the server. The release's own page put them back at its next save; this page never re-sends a change the server confirmed, so they stay out. It lasts as long as such a tab is open after the update — seconds: it reloads at its reconnect.
   - This page meeting a server without the ops door (a downgrade; the minute of an update) keeps its changes and sends them again; after 3 minutes of that it says once «These changes are not saved yet — the server does not take them (it may be restarting or older than this page); they are kept here while this page stays open», and «The changes kept on this page are saved now» when they land. On a downgrade they never land: closing or reloading the page loses them.
   - THIS page will not send a value larger than 16 384 characters (as JSON.stringify(value, null, 2) writes it, 8 spaces a line), a value nested deeper than 4 levels, a name longer than 4 096 characters, or a member past a group of 20 000 conversations.
    - It refuses them before any road carries them and says «This page did not keep a change (…)». No product writer reaches them: its largest value is 139 characters, its deepest 2 levels.
    - Master's roads — an older tab, an import, the ws rename — take them, as master does.
  - Two devices changing the same item within the time one request spends on its way (the network and the hub's queue — the incident's loop lagged 1.9 s): the hub orders them by their arrival less their ages, so the one that arrives later may stand, as on master.
  - A change made more than 7 days before it reaches the server (a laptop asleep for a week, then woken) is not applied: the page shows the server's state and says so where what it shows changed.
  - A page reloaded during a stall shows the server's state, which the first echoes roll back ON SCREEN until the acts the page sent before the reload land — they are on the wire and nothing is lost on the server; the screen catches up with the echoes.
  - A copy of a change that sat on the way while five other page loads changed the same item can be applied once more (a fact remembers four other pages).
  - A change that had to go again (its first send failed or was late), another device changing the same item, and a clock stepping FORWARD — the device's or the server's — after the earlier change and before the later change's copy is judged, by more than the time between the two changes: the earlier change can stand. (The age must follow the wall clock, or a laptop's sleep would make its old change look fresh.)
  - A hub restarted DURING a step back of its clock loses its idle time and its downtime (its mark cannot know them).
  - A forward jump of the hub's clock by more than 7 days, seen by one write, sweeps every fact: a beaten change's waiting copy can then land over the later change.
  - A state file put back from a backup carries its older clock mark: open pages refuse the restored life until they reload.
  - A device clock set BACK during a sleep in which its monotonic clock also stopped understates the change's age.
  - After a rollback to a release without facts and back, that release's writes left no facts.
  - A write walks the store as master's does — about 2.5× master's slope (19 ms at 20 000 conversations, master 6.6 ms).
  - A removal by a writer that carries no facts (an old tab's un-archive) is undone by ANY change still on its way that was made after the item's last recorded change — another page's too, even one made before the removal (the price of «an omission is not an act»; master's next whole-key push carried the item back the same way).
  - A fact written by a development build before round 9 (no released build wrote facts) names no ops: an id it names, sent again with other ops, applies.
  - Moving a conversation from one group to another through two separate changes is, for a moment, membership in both (nothing writes sessionGroups that way today).
   - A page that makes thousands of changes while the network is down spends page time on each: each change's request carries every unconfirmed one, up to 5 000, and the page copies its whole state for the view. 5 000 one-op changes cost the page about 36 s in all and 387–453 MiB — master's page 6.55 s and 68 MiB; a click takes about 14 ms with 5 000 waiting and 22 ms with 7 000 (master about 2.6 ms).
  - A hub that takes more than 2 min to answer a GET never satisfies a paced ask (each is given up at 2 min; they go on every 5 min). A waiting act's value stays on the row until a reconnect or a broadcast brings the state.
  - The facts grow with the slots changed in a week, and every write joins them all. 360 000 facts (180 000 items archived and un-archived in one week) make a one-op write 103 ms and the file 30 MiB. About 6 M facts would pass V8's longest string, and every write would fail until they age out.
  - Two different names longer than 128 characters with the same length and the same 64-bit digest would share a fact (one would be judged by the other's acts) — no product writer makes a name that long.
  - An old whole-key client (an older page) still erases per key what it SETS (it is old); a page of this release meeting an older server keeps its changes, sends them again while it stays open, and says so once.

A CLAIM, never a reading: its own provenance «person-reset», ONE writer (`src/usage-reset-claim.js`, data/usage-reset-claims.json); `POST /api/accounts/:id/reset-claim` bills nothing and calls no vendor (the client then presses the SAME ⟳ for that account). THE VIEW (`quotaModel.withResetClaim`): a claimed lane whose own reading is older than the claim and whose reset is later is viewed as reset at the claim — `windowDisplay` says reset-unconfirmed, `windowRemaining` 100, the pool ranks the member; the stored file is never touched.

Every quota reader goes through it — the chooser, `quotaVerdictFor`, the per-session pass and the pool switch (`maybePoolAutoSwitchForPool` kept its OWN copy of the reader, which read the bare file: a conversation placed on a claim was moved off it at the next tick — the copy is gone), `onMemberReadingFresh`, `notePoolAuthFailure`, the gather / removal / fallback verdicts. The engine reads of the usage cache that stay raw read STAMPS, not windows (the anchor sweep, the api-window sidecar, readRawUsageCache's overage facts, the wall's demotion line, onMemberReadingFresh's freshness gate, ownReading's lapse evidence) — the drill pins every read to one of those rows.

A lane's age is its typed window's `measuredAt` first, else the bucket's own stamp (`asOf` — the statusline's cap), else the file's clock for that family; a file-level `fetchedAt` never dates a lane a typed window dates (a 5h event no longer «contradicts» a weekly claim; a Fable banner no longer settles 5h / 7d).

The claim store settles on them; a reset is seen in them against the stored reading — the RAW PAIR before the merge, never the merged object (a late record stamped at arrival read as a reset), never a wall's mark (100 % with no proof a measuring producer wrote it last — the wall, the banner and the stream write exactly that), a repair or a view. ### account-reset-door K1 — the basis is a fact of ONE pool (主开发's read of the .397 tip c3215f7b5, 12:19Z; round 2, 13:12Z; the first pick after .397)
- **The finding (moderate; rebuilt: stands; the release does not have it).** On the .397 tip, `poolReadCache` decided raw-or-estimated per CALL, over the membership of the pool it was handed plus `also`.
  - The readers that hand no pool read an empty set: the verdict on a pool or a member scope, memberServable, the new-member wake and the gate's target check. So they estimated everyone except a member on its first learn, while the switch pass and the chooser read everyone raw.
  - Driven: the gate HELD a continue and re-armed it two hours out, on the very member the switch had kept the conversation on.
- **Round 1 (b05ea2098) went too wide, and is withdrawn.** It used one basis per CONNECTED SET of pools.
  - A learner in another pool that shares a member, even two hops away, put this pool raw.
  - A pool with no member list connected every pool to every other.
  - A conversation that runs directly on an account read raw, and fired on a member that its burn had spent.
- **THE LAW, round 2.** A decision compares the members of ONE pool, and every reading inside it stands on that pool's basis, decided by what THAT pool compares.
  - What a pool compares: its membership, read now, plus the ids its own last switch pass compared beyond it (the default's current member and each of its conversations' billing member).
  - Nothing another pool compares moves it. A member in two pools may read raw inside one pool's decision and estimated inside the other's at the same instant; no decision mixes.
  - **A reader that knows its pool names it** (`poolBasisRaw(poolId)` through `poolReadCache(poolId)`):
    - quotaVerdictFor on a pool scope reads that pool's basis;
    - a member scope asked for a pooled session reads the session's pool's basis: the gate's target check and the link's own verdict (`sessionPoolOf`);
    - memberServable for the For-you checking card reads the session's pool's basis;
    - the new-member wake reads each scope it fires in on that scope's basis.
  - **A reader with no pool reads as the release reads**: estimated where the estimator has an estimate. That covers a conversation that runs directly on an account, the projection's re-read and the Usage rings. That rule starts no turn and moves no conversation, and with nobody learning in a pool, that pool's every number is the release's.
  - Round 1's rings door, its 5 s look and `accounts.poolIds()` are gone; the rings are the release's.
- **ONE INSTANT, per pool.** A pool's fact is held for the rest of the synchronous run that read it, and kept 1 s across runs, while nothing it compares and nothing the estimator says has moved.
  - It is built again at once when the pool's id set changes (its membership, or its pass's compared ids), or when `basisGen` moves (rates landed, a fold threw).
  - A basis change the estimator does not announce is seen at the next build, within a second: the 60 s bound, a turn's cold-read budget, the ledger's load.
- **A FLIP.** A flip found by the pool's own pass is said by that pass («this pass decides on that basis»), and that pass decides on it. A flip found by any other reader is decided by a FORCED pass of that pool in the next turn, never inside the reader's run («the pool decides again on that basis»); a hot pool's move fires the armed continue. Both directions are decided.
  - The words are true after the 60 s bound too: «no id it compares holds it raw any more — its members are estimated again».
- **THE LINKS.** The switch pass reads each conversation's link and billing member once, after the cross asks settle, and its loop decides on those very reads.
  - A pass started inside the loop ends the reuse (`_passGen`), for example a fire whose gate runs at once.
  - Readers outside a pass read no link. readlinks per steady tick equal the release's: 243 at 8 members × 40 conversations, 249 at nine accounts in three pools (the .397 tip: 323 and 329).
- **What a person gets in the gate's run.** The target check, the forced re-decision, the final verdict and the link check run in one synchronous run after the gate's last await, so they read one fact.
  - A learn that lands DURING the gate's probe is seen by the run after it: on the newer fact the forced re-decision moves s1 to C, and the continue goes to C.
  - Should a learn land inside the run itself (a reader driving a fold slice), the fact is built again. The re-decision, the verdict and the link check then stand on the newer fact, and the person gets that one; the target check only decided whether to re-decide.
- **What the one basis costs in that minute.** The continue goes to the member the RAW reading allows: A, at 88 % read 2 h ago, though its burn says 96 %. The release would have gone to C. A refusal walls A for that conversation (SESSION_WALL_MS), and the next pass moves it.
- **Pins** (scripts/test-account-reset-door.mjs: legs one-basis, basis-flip, pool-own and switch-basis; the heavy controls row, ALL PASS 127):
  - **one-basis.** With C learning, the pool's reader reads A:88r B:50r C:30r. The chooser, the switch, the verdict and the gate all name A, with no re-arm. The pooled session's member scope equals the pool scope. A pool that shares B reads B:58e. A reader with no pool reads the release's numbers. With nobody learning, every number is the release's.
  - **basis-flip.** A learn landing during the gate's probe sends the continue to C. A landing no gate asks about is decided again, and said once. One run reads one fact, 2 s on its clock. basisGen moves.
  - **pool-own:**
    - a learner in another pool: P is estimated and decides as the release;
    - a pool with no member list reads raw, and a listed pool beside it reads estimated;
    - a direct conversation is HELD and re-armed, as on the release;
    - a flip's pass is forced, even right after a default switch;
    - a flip the pool's own pass finds is said once, with no second pass;
    - a reader that finds a flip moves nothing inside its run;
    - D, learning, joining inside the memo's second makes the next pass and the next reader decide raw, and the flip is said;
    - a pass started inside the loop: s2 moves once.
  - **switch-basis.** The default's link on a member the pool no longer lists is compared.
  - **RED trees:** b19f0ecdb (the release), c3215f7b5 (the gate HELD), and b05ea2098, ref account-reset-door-k1r1 (P raw because of Q's learner; the direct conversation fired).
  - **RED patches:** verdict-no-pool, no-gen, no-hold, no-kick, kick-unforced, kick-self, kick-sync, ids-unwatched, only-landing, no-passgen, flip-silent, default-not-compared, no-pass-ids, no-basis and local-copy. Each is RED on its own row.
  - **The verifiers' drivers on this tree** (copies, scratch under the lane), each equal to the release's decisions:

    - direct D1–D6;
    - xp: gate shared, chain and no-share; begin-neg;

### hub-loop-stalls — EVERY HOLD GETS ITS FIRST SAMPLE; THE INSTRUMENT IS NEVER THE HOLDER; THE LOOP BEFORE THE DISK (the owner's hub on .393, 20:09Z boot: its capture and its journal)
- **The reading — what the owner's capture said and what it was.** The automatic capture 40 s after the boot (20 s, 395 samples) said «12.4 % · Node.js internals … — 72 % through hr · src/server/loop-blame.js:51», and it was read as the instrument's own cost (8.2 %). It was not:
  - loop-blame.js is byte-identical since 2026-10-23;
  - all 34 samples on `hr` sit directly under a src caller of a sync fs call (`_loadArchive` src/jobs.js:291 ×6, `readJson` helper-transcripts ×5, `writeJsonAtomic` channel-store ×4, `parseClaudeAuth` ×3 …), the fs function itself already gone from the stack;
  - measured: one `process.hrtime.bigint()` 47 ns (`performance.now()` 50, `Date.now()` 53), the wrapper 0.18–0.23 µs a call, with the witness's hook 0.95–1.08 µs;
  - a restore at the owner's shape (625 MB of stores, 38 sessions) makes 13 112 wrapped calls in its busiest second and a median of 2 a second after it.
  So 1.6 s of `hr` would take ~35 million calls in 20 s. The samples are asks posted while a wrapped call slept and answered at the wrapper's first line after it.
- **The instrument is transparent.** `instrumentTrim` (src/loop-hold.js) drops the innermost run of the instrument's frames (loop-blame.js, sync-fs-witness.js, and the node frames among them) from a sample, so the time lands on the caller. A stack that is the instrument's alone (the witness's own timer) is kept whole.
  - The capture's ask reads the live slot at its post (`syncNow`: the wrapped call in flight). It books such a sample as «asleep in <the call>»: the owner's line now reads «… · asleep in readFileSync — 72 % through _loadArchive · src/jobs.js:291».
  - A hold's late answer names its caller the same way.
- **Every hold gets its first sample.** On the owner's hub 54 of 74 holds (214 of ~300 s) were «not sampled (20 holds were sampled in the last hour)»: the count of 20 an hour ran out in the minutes after the boot. The count is gone; what bounds the asks is what it protected:
  - no ask at ≥ 85 % of the heap limit (now for holds too, re-read at every step);
  - one ask in flight; no ask on a free loop (a hold is ≥ 1 s, its first sample ≤ ~2 ms);
  - a TIME budget for the later samples: their own measured main-thread runs under 36 s of the rolling hour (1 %). Past it a hold keeps its first sample and says «later samples not asked».
- **The loop before the disk.** «[local-index] the write … has not returned in 5 s — that disk is not answering» landed at the exact ends of 12.5 s, 6.5 s and 14 s LOOP holds on a local ext4 home: the write's answer could not run on the held loop.
  - The witness answers how long the main loop was held in a window (`loopHeld` / `loopHeldMs`, PURE `heldWithin`: the beat's own gap ring + the gap open now).
  - local-index asks it first: under the bound once the hold is taken out ⇒ «the main loop was held N s of it, so its answer could not run: the loop, not the disk».
- **Pins.**
  - test-loop-hold (fast, 147 → 154): 30 holds in a row ⇒ 30 sampled (2.369.395: 20); the gates that stay; the budget's rolling hour; the line past the budget; the trim on the owner's shape (through `sampleOf`); `heldWithin`; the worker's wiring. 10 red on 2.369.395.
  - test-cpu-capture (fast, 61 → 63): the capture's row for a sync-fs sleep, the control = the owner's exact line. 2 red on 2.369.395.
  - test-local-index (fast, 96 → 99): the loop's words, the disk's, the wiring. 3 red on 2.369.395.
  - test-loop-hold-live ③ (heavy): 30 holds in a row named; a budget of 0 ⇒ each its first sample.

### hub-loop-stalls follow-up to commit 3 — ONE READ, ONE WRITE IN FLIGHT, WHOEVER STARTED IT (the integration read of .393, 11:13Z)
- **The finding.** The CPU capture's `nameRaws` (src/server/sync-fs-witness-worker.js) cleared its one-read-in-flight guard (`naming`) when its reading time ran out while the stat / realpath / readFile was still pending, and set no slow hold. Each later capture started ANOTHER read of the same file: a hung network read held one more libuv threadpool thread per capture (the pool is the whole process's: four by default).
- **The law.** A read that has not returned is still in flight — one hung read, never more, whoever started it (a hold's names or a capture's). `readOne(rel)` is the one road for both: `naming` is cleared only when the read itself returns, and a read that took 100 ms or more starts the slow hold when it returns, whoever waited for it. A capture that finds a read pending says why its functions go by location alone: «a read of the install's files has not returned — one read waits, no other starts» (the reading time spent and a slow read have their own words).
- **The same law for the capture's file.** A write past its 10 s is still in flight: a capture that ends while it is pending writes nothing and says «the last capture's file … has not been written yet — the disk has not answered; one write waits, no other starts».
- **The leftover temp file (judged: removed).** A process killed inside the capture's write leaves «.<name>.<pid>.tmp», never renamed and never listed. `keptFiles` now removes such a file at the next kept write, except the one of a write in flight; no other name in the directory is touched (a reused pid's leftover too: at the prune no write of this thread is in flight).
- **Pins.** test-cpu-capture-live Ⓙ: a preload in the watchdog THREAD stands for the hung kernel call (each stat of the install's .js files left pending, counted). Four door captures start **one** read (a740aea7b: **4**); three captures against a write that never answers start **one** write, the next two «has not been written yet» (a740aea7b: **2**, the third door refused while the second write spent its 10 s). MUTANTS «the read's guard cleared at its budget» (4 reads) and «no guard on the capture's write» (2 writes) are red by name. test-cpu-capture (fast, 61 → 65): the leftover temp files, the words. On a740aea7b's module the same names drop no temp file.

### groups-sweep-on-change commit 2 — MEMBERSHIP IS AN INDEX (the owner's performance profile 2026-11-11: groupsForSession ≈ 5.2 s of the sweep chain)
- **Read:** `TaskGroupManager.groupsForSession` is asked per prompt (agent-routes prompt-context, server.js ctxGroupsOf), per roster build × every live session (roster-pass), per agent call / route (task-context, resolveAgentGroup, jobs, msg endpoints — every session per send) and per grant / mount check (mounts-plugins-wiring, spawn caps, automations, peer cards, apps access). Each ask walked every group and, per group, built the Context rows' cache key by serializing them.
- **The law.** (1) The index (`_memberIndex`) holds what membership reads — the unarchived groups in the answer's order, each one's session-key Set and its resolved discover folders — and a result map keyed by the call's own strings (`_memberAnswer`). (2) THE SPLIT OF THE REVISION, by what membership reads: a store write (`rev()`) asks `memberSig` (each record's key, id, archived, createdAt, sessions[], Context rows) and the records' identity; unchanged ⇒ the index stays (a progress line, a title, a note, a clear), changed ⇒ rebuilt — never a list of «membership writers» a later writer could forget. (3) The folders are the ones `_res` holds NOW: the index keeps the very cache entry they came from and re-derives them when it is gone or past its 4 s bound — a folder made on disk is seen at the same ask as the walk. (4) The result map holds at most `MEMBER_RESULTS_MAX` (2 048) asks between two rebuilds — one per (session key, cwd + realpath, spawned-into ids) asked: every live and discovered session × its cwds — and is cleared at the cap. (5) ON ANY DOUBT THE WALK ANSWERS (`_groupsForSessionWalk`, the old code verbatim), said nowhere: a call shape the index does not key, a record that is not an object or whose createdAt is not a number, any throw while the index is read or built. A stat that throws (EACCES), a symlink loop as a cwd, a cwd that no longer exists are the walk's own answers (`_kindOf` ⇒ missing; `_realOf` ⇒ the cwd alone), and the index reads the same `_res` / `_realOf`.
- **Measured on the owner's live store (read-only):** progress lines 0.28 a minute over 24 h (0.34 over 6 h, at most 4 in a minute over 7 days); the store file written 4 times in 10 minutes. The split keeps the index across them: a write that moves nothing membership reads costs the next ask one signature (67 µs at the owner's shape).
